posts.text:
Pickleball shoes are not tennis shoes with a different logo, and the difference is where people get hurt.

Pickleball lives in a smaller box. More stops, more starts, more short lateral scrambles, far less of the long sliding recovery tennis asks for. So the outsole wants immediate grip rather than controlled slide, and the upper wants lateral lockdown more than heel drag protection.

Wear a running shoe on a pickleball court often enough and your ankles will eventually send you the invoice.

The Selkirk CourtStrike Pro 3.0 is the one that leaves here most often. $128, men's and women's, full size runs in stock.

posts.text:
16x19 or 18x20? The question behind half the racquet advice on the internet.

Open pattern, 16x19: fewer cross strings, so the bed moves more, bites more and launches higher. More spin, more forgiveness, more depth for free.

Dense pattern, 18x20: strings move less, the ball comes off flatter and lower. Less spin, but the shot goes where you aimed it, every time.

The honest rule is that it follows your swing, not your level. Big western grip, heavy topspin, long finish? Open. Flatter, more compact, drive through the ball? Dense.

The Blade 98 V10 comes both ways at $299, which makes it a genuinely useful frame to settle the argument with.

16x19: https://www.racquetpoint.com/products/wilson-blade-98-16x19-v10-tennis-racquet
18x20: https://www.racquetpoint.com/products/wilson-blade-98-18x20-v10-tennis-racquet

posts.text:
14mm or 16mm? The pickleball question that gets the most confused answers.

Core thickness is a trade between power and control. A 14mm core is stiffer and more explosive, so the ball leaves faster and drives come easier. A 16mm core has more cushion, which means more dwell time, better touch at the kitchen and a bigger effective sweet spot.

Rough guide. If you win points by driving and you already have pace, 14. If you win points at the net with dinks, resets and patience, 16.

Most improving players are better served by 16 than they expect, because control problems cost more points than a lack of power ever does.

Holbrook Pro Aero comes in both at $169.99.

https://www.racquetpoint.com/products/holbrook-pro-aero-t-elongated-pickleball-paddle-14mm-16mm

Selkirk's pitch for the CourtStrike Pro 3.0 is three words: lighter, quicker, cooler.

Worth unpacking, because "new version" usually means "new colourway".

The 3.0 is genuinely a lighter and better ventilated build than the 2.0, and Selkirk's own line is that they did it without giving up longevity or comfort. That last part is the bit that matters. Plenty of shoes get lighter by getting flimsier, and you find out in month three when the upper starts separating at the toe.

If you play in the heat, or you play long sessions, the ventilation is the upgrade you will actually notice. If your 2.0s are still going strong, there is no urgency here and we would rather you wore them out first.

$128, men's and women's.

Tension, briefly, since it comes up more than anything else.

Tighter strings give you control and less power. Looser strings give you power, comfort and more dwell time on the ball. That is the whole trade.

Most people are strung tighter than they need to be, usually because someone told them a number in 2011 and they have repeated it ever since. If your arm aches and your shots land short, dropping two or three pounds is free and often fixes both.

We are mail in and you pick the tension when you order. If you want a recommendation, tell us what the ball is doing and we will suggest one.

posts.text:
The SLK ERA Power comes in two shapes, and picking the wrong one is the most common mistake we see.

Elongated gives you reach and leverage. The extra length at the top of the face means more on drives and a longer arm at full stretch, and you pay for it with a narrower sweet spot. It rewards players who are already finding the middle.

Widebody spreads the same surface area sideways instead. Bigger, more forgiving face, easier to control at the kitchen, slightly less reach.

Rough guide. If you still catch the edge guard more often than you would like, widebody. If your contact is clean and you want free power, elongated.

$200 either way. Cyan, White, Volt and Regal in both shapes, plus Purple in widebody.

https://www.racquetpoint.com/products/selkirk-slk-era-power-pickleball-paddle

posts.text:
Regular duty or extra duty? It is the question we get asked most about balls, and the answer is not the one people expect.

It has nothing to do with how hard you hit. It is about the court.

Extra duty has a thicker, woolier felt that survives abrasive hard courts. Put it on clay or an indoor carpet and the felt picks up the surface, fluffs up and plays heavy and slow.

Regular duty has a thinner felt. It is the right ball for clay and indoor. Put it on a rough hard court and it will shred in a set and a half.

Most people buy whatever is on the shelf and then wonder why the balls died so fast, or why they felt like lead. That is usually all it is.

Dunlop balls from $4.79.

Twenty nine Tecnifibre frames on the shelf, and almost everyone walks in asking the wrong question first. It is not which racquet is best. It is which of the three families you belong to.

Fire. Open 16x19 pattern, easy to swing, built to help you get the ball up and dipping. If you play with topspin and want the frame working with you, start here. Fire 270 $229, Fire 285 $249, Fire 300 $259, Fire 305S $269, and the 260 OS at $239 if you want the bigger head.

T-Fight. The players' frame. Tighter feel, more direct, rewards you for swinging properly and does not flatter a lazy ball. T-Fight 270 $229 through the 315S at $279.

TF-40. Tour control, and it makes no apology for it. It hands you nothing for free, but you will always know exactly where the ball is going. That is Rinderknech's frame. From $249 for the 290 16M.

Not sure? Tell us what happens when you miss. If your balls sail long, you want more control. If they land short, you want more help. That one answer usually narrows it to a single racquet.

Every frame ships strung with your choice of string and tension, done in house.

Sport Series 14mm, $59.99. Your first real paddle. Not a toy, not a compromise, just the honest entry point.

Pro Aero, $169.99. Elongated, hybrid or square, in 14mm or 16mm. Pick the shape to match how you play, not what looks fastest.
